reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Swelling over the front of the kneecap from inflammation of the superficial prepatellar bursa
Classically related to prolonged or repetitive kneeling, hence 'housemaid's knee'
As with the olecranon bursa, the superficial position makes it prone to septic bursitis
Distinguishing septic from aseptic bursitis is the priority; warmth, erythema, fever and disproportionate pain suggest infection
Aspiration for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy guides management when infection is suspected
The knee joint itself is usually uninvolved and joint range is typically preserved

Aseptic cases are managed with avoidance of kneeling, protection and aspiration if symptomatic, with corticosteroid injection reserved for resistant aseptic cases and avoided when infection is possible
reference.pathophysiology: The prepatellar bursa lies superficially between the skin and the patella, allowing the skin to glide over the kneecap. Repetitive kneeling, friction or a direct blow provokes inflammation and effusion. Its superficial location makes it vulnerable to inoculation and infection, particularly through breaks in the overlying skin and typically with skin organisms such as staphylococci. Systemic causes such as gout and rheumatoid disease can also inflame the bursa. Because the bursa does not communicate with the knee joint, intra-articular structures are usually spared.
additionalDifferentials: Knee joint effusion or intra-articular pathology
additionalInvestigations: Bursal aspiration for cell count, Gram stain and culture
Inflammatory markers, with blood cultures if systemically unwell
Ultrasound to confirm a superficial bursal collection separate from the joint
Plain radiographs if fracture or a foreign body is suspected
redFlags: Fever, spreading erythema and severe pain suggesting septic bursitis or cellulitis
A tense joint effusion or inability to bear weight suggesting intra-articular pathology
reference.prognosis: Aseptic prepatellar bursitis usually resolves with protection and activity change, recurring if kneeling continues; septic bursitis typically responds to antibiotics and drainage.
pitfalls: Injecting a potentially infected bursa with corticosteroid
Confusing a superficial bursal swelling with a true knee joint effusion
Not analysing aspirate when infection is suspected
Overlooking a foreign body or penetrating injury
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
